title: Mariachi: The Rodney Dangerfield of Music
summary: Josh and Chuck explore mariachi music, starting from Josh's pick. They cover its origins in colonial Mexico with Spanish, African, and indigenous influences, the Jalisco son jalisciense roots, haciendas and the Mexican Revolution, the disputed etymology of the word (the Cora word for a tree, versus the French "mariage" myth), the shift to Mexico City in the 1910s-20s with bigger ensembles, horns, and charro suits, busking and restaurant performance, instruments (vihuela, guitarrón, violins, trumpets), genres (ranchera, corrido, son jalisciense, huapango, zapateado), UNESCO recognition in 2011, Chicano movement and Linda Ronstadt's 1987 album, spread to Yugoslavia and abroad, notable groups (Mariachi Vargas, Mariachi Los Camperos, Mariachi Cobra at Epcot), and women in mariachi. The episode closes with listener mail about the Somerton Man case being solved through DNA.
topics: Linda Ronstadt Canciones de mi Padre

segments.title: Opening banter and Josh's mariachi pick
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the Mexican Hat Dance from kindergarten and Josh's love of mariachi, sparked by his time living in a Mexican neighborhood in LA. They discuss how mariachi has kept a consistent sound over generations and its uneven respect globally, tied to xenophobia and class attitudes.

segments.title: Origins in colonial Mexico and Jalisco
segments.summary: The hosts trace mariachi to colonial Mexico, blending Spanish, enslaved African, and indigenous rhythmic traditions. Early farm-worker string ensembles in Jalisco played son jalisciense, with violin, guitar, and harp before horns were added.

segments.title: Haciendas, the Mexican Revolution, and Cocula
segments.summary: Mariachi performers were peasant workers on haciendas under a feudal-like system. The hosts describe how exploitation led to the Mexican Revolution, and mention Cocula, where an 1852 letter from a Catholic priest is the first written record of the music.

segments.title: Etymology of the word mariachi
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the disputed origin of the word mariachi. They debunk the myth that it derives from the French word for marriage, linked to the French occupation of Mexico from 1862 to 1866. They favor a Cora word for a wood used for instruments, and note a religious Virgin Mary theory they doubt.

segments.title: Migration to Mexico City and the charro suit
segments.summary: Displaced musicians moved to Mexico City in the 1910s and 1920s, where regional styles blended. Bands grew larger, horns were added, and musicians adopted charro suits. Performers began busking in public places and moving around restaurants.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break; hosts banter about charro suits and Nudy suits before the break.

segments.title: Instruments and genres
segments.summary: The hosts describe the vihuela, the guitarrón, violins, and trumpets, and the German-influenced waltzes and polkas. They cover genres including huapango, ranchera, corrido, and the song Volver Volver by Vicente Fernández, and the ballad versus corrido distinction.

segments.title: UNESCO recognition, Chicano movement, and Linda Ronstadt
segments.summary: The hosts cover UNESCO's 2011 listing of mariachi on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list, mariachi's traditional oral transmission, the Chicano movement and songs like El Picote, and Linda Ronstadt's 1987 album Canciones de mi Padre.

segments.title: Global spread: Yugoslavia and other countries
segments.summary: Mexican cinema spread mariachi worldwide. The hosts describe its popularity in Yugoslavia, where it was seen as politically neutral, and mention mariachi bands in Japan, China, and Sweden.

segments.title: Notable mariachi groups and women in mariachi
segments.summary: The hosts name notable groups, including Mariachi Vargas, Mariachi Los Camperos, and Mariachi Cobra at Epcot, plus trumpet innovators. They discuss women in mariachi, including Rosa Quirino and all-female groups, and a 2013 study on gender expectations.

segments.title: Listener mail: Somerton Man solved
segments.summary: A listener from Adelaide reports that DNA matching has identified the Somerton Man as Carl Webb, an engineer and instrument maker from Melbourne.
